clue.text: An old copper isn't a handy item

parts.note: something not near to hand is far away
an item is a thing

explanation.surface: A worn old coin is no use to anyone, so not worth keeping in your pocket.
explanation.walkthrough: A FARTHING was a small British copper coin worth a quarter of an old penny, withdrawn in 1960. Read the rest as FAR THING: an item that is far away is not handy.
explanation.definitionFit: The farthing was a low-value British coin made of copper or bronze, so it is literally an old copper.

clue.text: Sacked a politician as underground risk

parts.note: sacked from a job
taken as written
Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: Losing a parliamentary seat counts as a hazard, like working in a mine.
explanation.definitionFit: Firedamp is methane gas in coal mines, which can explode underground, a major hazard for miners.

clue.text: They chew things over to break down spirit in workers

definitions.text: They chew things over to break down

parts.note: rum is a spirit
taken as written
worker ants are crossword's usual workers

explanation.surface: Factory staff chewing over a dispute that has broken down their morale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chew things over' suggests thinking hard, but here it is literal: cud-chewing animals bring food back up to grind it down further.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruminants such as cows and sheep regurgitate and rechew their food to digest it fully.

clue.text: Therefore scram!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: for this reason, as a consequence
second meaning: an old command to go away from here

explanation.definitionFit: Hence means as a result, and in older English 'Hence!' was an order to leave at once.

clue.text: Medicine for Mussolini's mare

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the word that followed mare in Mussolini's slogan for the Mediterranean

explanation.surface: A dose prescribed for the dictator's horse.
explanation.walkthrough: Mare is not a horse but Latin for sea: Mussolini called the Mediterranean 'mare nostrum', our sea, the Roman name for it.
explanation.definitionFit: A nostrum is a patent medicine of doubtful worth, and also the Latin word for 'our'.

clue.text: Result of flak

parts.note: surface reading: the consequence of anti-aircraft fire or of fierce criticism
setter's reading: flak is shot fired upwards, so the whole thing is a shot that goes up

explanation.walkthrough: Flak is anti-aircraft fire, aimed up at planes. Split the answer as UP SHOT and it describes flak itself, while the whole word means a result.
explanation.definitionFit: An upshot is the final outcome or consequence of something, which is what a result is.

clue.text: Fixes food to suit pattern

parts.note: to pin something is to fix it in place
tripe is the stomach lining of cattle, eaten as food

explanation.surface: Someone adjusts a meal to fit a set plan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suit' looks like a verb meaning to fit, but it is the noun: a man's suit.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinstripe is the thin-lined fabric design classic in business suits, so a suit pattern.

clue.text: Jute — as not all authors agree

indicators.note: not all of the following words is used, only a run of letters lying inside them

parts.note: the letters run across the join between the two words

explanation.surface: A remark that writers disagree about the Jutes.
explanation.walkthrough: Jute looks like the sacking fibre, but it is a member of the Jutes, a Germanic people from Jutland. Hengist and HORSA are said to have led them into Kent in the 5th century, and many scholars doubt Horsa existed, which the surface slyly admits.
explanation.definitionFit: Horsa is the semi-legendary Jutish chieftain who with his brother Hengist supposedly invaded Kent, so he is a Jute.

clue.text: Suitable West End mourning wear? Surely not

definitions.text: Suitable West End mourning wear? Surely not

parts.note: surface reading: proper funeral clothing for smart central London; setter's reading: suit material and weeds
rough country cloth would be quite wrong for a smart London funeral, hence the denial

explanation.walkthrough: Mourning wear is widow's weeds, and TWEEDS contains the weeds while being suit cloth (suit-able). The West End is London's smart district, where tweeds would not be worn to mourn.
explanation.definitionFit: Tweeds are suits of rough woollen country cloth, the opposite of formal black town mourning clothes.

clue.text: Maxims for our times

parts.note: Anno Domini, the label of our present era
ages are periods of time

explanation.surface: Wise sayings suited to the modern world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Our times' reads as AD AGES: AD marks the years of the Christian era we live in.
explanation.definitionFit: An adage is a traditional saying expressing a general truth, a synonym for a maxim.

clue.text: Having undergone normal-type conversion?

parts.note: setter's reading: text reset into roman, the ordinary upright typeface used for normal printing
second reading: converted to the Roman Catholic faith

explanation.walkthrough: In printing, roman is the normal upright type, as opposed to italic. Text put into roman type has been ROMANISED, and so has a convert to the Catholic Church.
explanation.definitionFit: To romanise is to put into roman type or roman letters, or to bring someone into the Roman Church.

clue.text: It conveys a sense of cool courage

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a fibre carrying sensation from the body to the brain
second meaning: steady boldness under pressure

explanation.surface: Something passes on a feeling of calm bravery.
explanation.definitionFit: Nerves carry sensory signals through the body, and the word also names composure and bravery in a tight spot.

clue.text: Poet is soundly swindled

indicators.note: soundly here means by sound, so the next word is judged by how it is pronounced

parts.note: to be done is slang for being cheated

explanation.surface: A poet has been thoroughly cheated.
explanation.walkthrough: John DONNE, the 17th-century English poet, is pronounced like DONE, as in 'I've been done'.
explanation.definitionFit: John Donne was an English metaphysical poet, so the name is an example of a poet.

clue.text: The drive of the Britisher

parts.note: surface reading: the ambition or energy of a British person
setter's reading: which side the steering wheel is on in British cars

explanation.walkthrough: Britain drives on the left, so its cars put the steering wheel on the side opposite the kerb: they are RIGHT-HAND drive.
explanation.definitionFit: British vehicles have the steering wheel mounted on the right, so their drive is right-hand.

clue.text: For thirty seconds one has quiet at least

definitions.note: adverbial phrase for a noun used in phrases such as 'at a minimum'

parts.note: half a minute, here the first half of the word minute; MIN is also its abbreviation
the Roman numeral for one
to keep mum is to stay quiet

explanation.surface: Someone stays silent for at least half a minute.
explanation.walkthrough: Thirty seconds is half a minute, and the clue takes the half literally: the first three of the six letters of minute.
explanation.definitionFit: The minimum is the least amount possible, so 'at least' points to it as the lowest acceptable level.

clue.text: Island birds with anthropomorphic roots

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase for a plural noun: plants that have such roots

parts.note: the Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea
drakes are male ducks

explanation.surface: Birds on an island whose ancestry traces back to humans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roots' suggests ancestry, but it is literal: the forked root of the mandrake looks like a human figure.
explanation.definitionFit: The mandrake plant has a forked root resembling a human body, the source of many legends.

clue.text: A piper's accidents?

parts.note: surface reading: mishaps, things knocked over
setter's reading: a piper is a pipe smoker, who lights up with thin tapers of wood or paper

explanation.walkthrough: A piper here smokes a pipe rather than playing one. SPILLS are the slips of wood or twisted paper used to light a pipe, and spills are also accidents.
explanation.definitionFit: Spills means accidental falls or upsets, and also the paper or wooden tapers used for lighting a pipe.

clue.text: One may be prone to take things so

definitions.text: One may be prone to take things so

parts.note: surface reading: someone inclined to accept setbacks passively
setter's reading: prone means stretched out face down, so a prone person is literally horizontal

explanation.walkthrough: To take things LYING DOWN is to accept them without protest; a person lying prone is doing exactly that, literally.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for meekly accepting bad treatment matches the literal posture of someone stretched flat on the ground.

clue.text: Make a recovery and the game won't be lost

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to get something back or put a situation right
second meaning: a gun dog fetches shot birds so none go missing

explanation.surface: A sporting comeback keeps the match from being lost.
explanation.walkthrough: The game is not a match but shot birds; a retriever dog brings them back so they are not lost.
explanation.definitionFit: To retrieve is to recover or regain something, and to fetch killed game, which is what retriever dogs do.

clue.text: Interesting practice, given frequent Rialto rating

definitions.text: Interesting practice, given frequent Rialto rating

parts.note: setter's reading: the practice of lending money at interest, and an old word for custom
allusion: in The Merchant of Venice Shylock says Antonio has many a time scolded him on the Rialto over his moneylending

explanation.walkthrough: The Merchant of Venice: Shylock complains he has often been scolded on the Rialto, Venice's business district, over his moneylending. USANCE means both usury and custom.
explanation.definitionFit: Usance is an archaic word for both lending at interest and an established custom or practice.

clue.text: They happen to find an opening in two quarters

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another, here inside the pair of compass points

parts.note: east and south, two of the compass quarters
a vent is an opening that lets air out

explanation.surface: People chance upon a gap in two districts of a city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quarters' suggests city districts, but here it means compass points.
explanation.definitionFit: Events are occurrences, things that take place or happen.

clue.text: Top engineer needs implement to make a crack

parts.note: Commander Royal Engineers, the senior engineer officer in a British Army formation
a vice is a clamping tool

explanation.surface: A senior engineer needs a tool to break something open.
explanation.walkthrough: CRE is a British Army abbreviation for Commander, Royal Engineers. A vice is the bench tool that grips work.
explanation.definitionFit: A crevice is a narrow opening or fissure in rock or a wall, a synonym for a crack.

clue.text: Big bottles among Bizet's juvenilia?

indicators.note: juvenilia are works of youth, so the grown-ups in the opera's title are swapped for youngsters

parts.note: Bizet's best-known opera

explanation.surface: Large flasks found among a composer's early works.
explanation.walkthrough: Take Bizet's opera CARMEN and make it juvenile: the MEN become BOYS, giving CARBOYS.
explanation.definitionFit: Carboys are large glass or plastic bottles, often in a protective frame, used for acids or liquids.

clue.text: Watch Nimrod!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a pocket watch with a hinged metal lid protecting the glass
second meaning: Nimrod in Genesis is 'a mighty ... before the Lord'

explanation.definitionFit: A hunter is a pocket watch with a protective cover, and Nimrod is the Bible's archetypal hunter.

clue.text: Make insufficient use of briefs, for instance?

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read as two words: to wear something too little
second meaning: garments worn beneath outer clothes, of which briefs are one kind

explanation.surface: A lawyer is not making the most of the cases handed to them.
explanation.walkthrough: Briefs suggest a barrister's cases, but they are short underpants. Split the answer as UNDER-WEAR and it means to wear too little.
explanation.definitionFit: Underwear is clothing worn next to the skin, with briefs as an example, signalled by 'for instance'.

clue.text: A man needs this tropical kit to get a baboon

definitions.text: A man needs this tropical kit to get a baboon

parts.note: a hard-wearing cotton twill used for uniforms in hot climates
setter's reading: add this word to the letters of man and you have a large West African baboon

explanation.walkthrough: DRILL is the cotton cloth of tropical uniforms. Put MAN in front of it and you get MANDRILL, the baboon; a drill is itself a baboon too.
explanation.definitionFit: Drill is a heavy twilled cotton for tropical uniforms, and the drill is also a baboon closely related to the mandrill.

clue.text: Its north wall elevation is to scale

definitions.text: Its north wall elevation is to scale

parts.words: north wall elevation is to scale
parts.note: surface reading: an architect's drawing of a building's north side, drawn to scale
setter's reading: a mountain whose famous north face is there to be climbed

explanation.walkthrough: An elevation sounds like an architect's drawing, but here it is height. The north face of the EIGER in the Swiss Alps is one of climbing's great challenges.
explanation.definitionFit: The Eiger is a Swiss Alpine peak whose north face, the Nordwand, is a celebrated and deadly climb.

clue.text: What might there be to put you out?

definitions.text: What might there be to put you out?

indicators.note: what might it be asks what the word could become, inviting a rearrangement

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Someone asks what in a room could knock them unconscious.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition, and its word there is also the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Ether was once the standard anaesthetic, used to make patients unconscious before surgery.

clue.text: Magician's spell?

parts.note: surface reading: an incantation cast by a wizard
setter's reading: a spell is a turn or stint, and a magician's turn consists of illusions

explanation.walkthrough: Spell can mean a period of duty, and a TRICK is a sailor's spell at the helm; it is also what a conjuror performs.
explanation.definitionFit: A trick is a conjuror's illusion and also a stint of duty, as in a sailor's trick at the wheel.

clue.text: Saw feature some might describe as tasteful

parts.note: a saw blade's cutting edge is made of teeth
taken as written

explanation.surface: A saw's design is praised by some people as elegant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tasteful' suggests good taste, but here it means full of flavour.
explanation.definitionFit: Toothsome means delicious or good to eat, so tasteful in the sense of full of taste.

clue.text: "Some act That has no — of salvation in't" (Hamlet)

definitions.text: "Some act That has no — of salvation in't" (Hamlet)

parts.words: "Some act That has no — of salvation in't"
parts.note: a line from Hamlet with one word blanked out for the solver to supply
Hamlet, Act 3 Scene 3, as he decides to kill Claudius later, in some sinful act

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: Hamlet waits to kill Claudius at 'some act that has no RELISH of salvation in't', so his soul will be damned.
explanation.definitionFit: Relish here means a trace or flavour, so the act has not even a taste of salvation.

clue.text: Almost all greatness, if misapplied, will make enemies

definitions.note: a verb that takes an object, as in 'make enemies of'

indicators.note: misapplied means put to the wrong use or wrongly arranged, so the letters are reordered
almost all means one short of the whole, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written, before its last letter goes

explanation.surface: Power used badly turns people against you.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the final S of greatness and the eight remaining letters rearrange into ESTRANGE.
explanation.definitionFit: To estrange people is to alienate them, turning friends into enemies or strangers.
